title: Can a simple activation anomaly score (without training a probe) detect jailbreaks?

original_idea.problem: Whether unsupervised anomaly detection on activations works comparably to supervised probes for jailbreak detection is untested.
original_idea.direction: Collect activations from benign and jailbreak prompts. Compute per-dimension z-scores. Use L2 norm as anomaly score. Compare AUROC vs. supervised probe.
original_idea.why_it_matters: An unsupervised detector requiring zero labeled data would be truly 'almost free' and deployable immediately on new models.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: zero-label detection -> deployable on new models without data collection -> practical safety improvement at scale. Clear, defensible impact if the approach works (or useful negative result if it doesn't).

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires activation extraction and statistical analysis (z-scores, L2 norms). Conceptually straightforward but activation hooks and comparison methodology need intermediate ML skills.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: one AUROC comparison table (unsupervised vs supervised). Clear methodology: collect activations, compute z-scores, compare. Few dependencies.

novelty.reasoning: This idea is substantially addressed by recent work. ALERT (arXiv:2601.03600, Jan 2026) proposes zero-shot jailbreak detection via internal discrepancy amplification — no labeled attack data required. 'Learning to Detect Unknown Jailbreak Attacks' (arXiv:2508.09201, 2025) formulates jailbreak detection as anomaly detection using Multi-modal Safety Concept Activation Vectors (MSCAV) trained only on safe samples. 'LLM Jailbreak Detection for (Almost) Free!' (EMNLP 2025) explicitly frames unsupervised detection as nearly free. The proposed L2-norm z-score approach is simpler than these methods but the core question — can unsupervised anomaly detection on activations work without labels? — is answered affirmatively by existing work, with more sophisticated methods already published.
